heading: Small things I'm building
intro: Each one does one job well. Beeline does things on my Mac, Observatory keeps watch, Career Bridge asks people how they use AI at work, cube·type turns a Rubik’s cube into a typing game, and one more is on the way.

projects.name: Beeline
projects.tagline: Type or talk to your Mac, and a small bee shows where it acts.
projects.summary: A Mac assistant I open with ⌘Space. I type, or hold the keys and talk, and it opens things, changes settings, presses buttons and runs short plans.

hero.alt: The Beeline bar searching for wifi, with Open Wi-Fi as the top hit and actions to turn Wi-Fi off or on

sections.title: What it does
body: Beeline opens apps, files, tabs and System Settings pages from everyday words like “night shift”. It also runs menu commands, presses buttons in the app in front, tiles windows, converts units and currencies, and handles file chores like compressing or moving what’s selected in Finder.

Holding ⌘Space turns the search field into a microphone. My words fill the bar as I speak, and Return runs the top result. For bigger requests it asks Claude for a short plan, shows every step, and runs nothing until I approve it.

sections.title: The bee
body: Before Beeline presses something, a small drawn bee flies from the bar to the button, menu or window, a ring settles on the target, and a label says what is about to happen. My real pointer never moves.

Escape stops a run from any app, and clicking or typing myself takes over. Anything that can’t be undone, like emptying the Trash, pressing Send or a dialog’s OK, needs Return twice, and the card says exactly what it will touch.

sections.title: Where it came from
body: Voice control started as a separate prototype. I folded it into Beeline so there is one bar for typing and talking, and kept only the parts that held up: the on-screen cursor idea and a safe way to stop.

gallery.alt: A three-step plan in the Beeline bar: put Notes on the left, turn Wi-Fi off, keep the Mac awake, with Cancel and Run buttons
gallery.caption: Bigger requests become a plan I approve first.

gallery.alt: A currency conversion shown as a large answer in the Beeline bar
gallery.caption: Quick answers appear right in the bar.

highlights: Uses Apple’s on-device model for loose requests, and learns what I pick
Watches Escape to stop a run without ever swallowing the key
Runs on the Mac; goes online only for currency rates and requests I send to Claude

connects.text: Plans come from Claude, and Observatory shows how much of that usage is left.

projects.name: Observatory
projects.kind: Menu bar app · Mac and Windows
projects.tagline: A calm menu bar companion that watches my AI limits, agents, time and cost.
projects.summary: One glance tells me how much of my Claude Code and Codex limits is left, which agents are waiting on me, where my screen time went, and what the day cost. It runs on my own computer and never touches any of them.

hero.alt: The Observatory dashboard with fictional data: tiles for limits, agents, screen time and cost, then the Limits page

sections.title: Four questions
body: Observatory answers four things at a glance: am I near my limits, what are my agents doing, where did my time go, and what did it cost. The menu bar shows one number, the lowest limit left, with an amber dot when an agent is waiting on me.
The dashboard opens in my browser and breaks each answer down: limit windows with reset times and pace, screen time by app and category, and tokens priced at public API rates.

sections.title: An agents panel
body: The Agents page lists every Claude Code session as working, waiting on me, idle or done, with recent Codex jobs beside them. It reads only the small status files those tools already keep, never transcripts or job output.

sections.title: Monitor only
body: It never starts, stops or answers an agent, and it never changes the tools it reads. It sends nothing to any server and has no telemetry. Saved data holds totals and status, never prompts, messages or window titles.
Unknown is never shown as zero, and dollar figures are labeled as estimates, not bills.

sections.title: One computer first
body: Setup is one command. It builds the dashboard and a small menu bar app on my own computer and starts them at login, with no account and no installer. A Mac and a Windows PC can optionally share one view over SSH, with combined sums clearly labeled.

gallery.alt: The Observatory Agents page with fictional data: sessions on two computers labeled Waiting on you, Working, Idle and Done
gallery.caption: The Agents panel across two computers, with fictional data.

highlights: Claude Code and Codex get equal weight everywhere
Screen time from ActivityWatch, grouped by app and category
Tests plant fake prompts and keys and check none reach saved data
MIT licensed, with a demo that uses fictional data

connects.text: Keeps an eye on the agents and limits behind Beeline’s plans.

projects.name: Career Bridge
projects.tagline: A short survey that asks Massachusetts workers and employers how AI shows up in their jobs.
projects.summary: Built for the Human Edge Studio datathon by SG+I, where it won 3rd place. Job ads show what employers ask for, not what people in the job do with AI, so Career Bridge asks them and publishes only totals.

hero.alt: The Career Bridge home page asking how people in these jobs actually use AI, above a What we found section

sections.title: The gap
body: About 526,000 Massachusetts workers are in jobs where AI overlaps with much of the work, yet under 1% of job ads for those jobs mention AI skills. That comes from the Lightcast AI Exposure Index, 2025 job ads and BLS worker counts.
Ads can’t tell the difference between a job that doesn’t need AI and one where people already use it and nobody is asking. Asking people can.

sections.title: The survey
body: Workers take five minutes to mark which work activities they do in a typical week and whether AI helps with each. Employers take three to say what the role needs and what is becoming more important.

The activities come from O*NET, so answers line up with federal data, plus three AI activities O*NET doesn’t track yet. It starts with three jobs: administrative assistants, customer service representatives and retail salespeople.

sections.title: Results and job pages
body: Results show only totals by job and region, and any group with fewer than 10 responses is hidden. The page points out where workers and employers differ, which shows who could use AI training.
Career counselors can look up any job for pay, growth, training, how much AI is already used on the work, and nearby jobs with similar skills. Every number names its source.

sections.title: Status
body: A working prototype. All survey results in the demo are sample data. It’s an independent student project, not affiliated with MassHire, Lightcast or the Commonwealth of Massachusetts.

gallery.alt: The survey start page with three jobs, each with I do this job and I hire for this job buttons
gallery.caption: Workers and employers pick a job to start.

gallery.alt: A job page for administrative assistants with workers, median pay, yearly change, training and a 0 to 100 AI use scale
gallery.caption: A job page for career counselors, with a source on every number.

highlights: 3rd place at Human Edge Studio by SG+I, October 2026
Built on O*NET work activities, so answers match federal data
Totals only, with groups under 10 responses hidden
Public data from BLS OEWS, O*NET 31.0 and the Anthropic Economic Index

projects.name: cube·type
projects.tagline: Solve a Rubik’s cube by typing words.
projects.summary: Every turn of the cube has a word: type rush and the right face turns, type recoil and it turns back. It plays in the browser and keeps stats like a typing test.

hero.alt: The cube·type game: a scrambled 3D cube in the middle, with a word beside each face, such as rover for R and relax for R prime

sections.title: How it plays
body: The first letter of a word is its face, words about going forward turn clockwise, and words about going back turn counter-clockwise. Enter repeats the last turn, so a word then Enter is a double. Swiping or the arrow keys rotate the whole cube.
The bar at the top tracks each stage of a CFOP solve. Once the first two layers are done, the last-layer algorithm shows up as a line of words to type, like a Monkeytype test.

sections.title: Three modes
body: Drill shows one move at a time and asks for its word. Sprint is one timed solve with splits. Zen is untimed, and new cubes keep coming.
Typing is never corrected. Wrong letters stay in red until I delete them, and a turn happens only when the word is exact.

sections.title: Choosing the words
body: Each move has a pool of words, and a picker chooses which one shows. Like Monkeytype it is mostly random, but it leans toward short words that switch hands and avoid using the same finger twice in a row.
It also counts finesse, borrowed from Tetris: turns that cancel out, like R then R prime, are wasted, and the game flags them.

gallery.alt: Drill mode showing R prime in large letters above the cube, with its word relax highlighted on the right
gallery.caption: Drill asks for one move at a time.

highlights: Stats for best time, average of 5 and 12, splits and finesse, saved in the browser
Eight camera views, and words move to sit beside their faces
Four themes, including the classic Monkeytype look
